The vector $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of a $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $2.$ Find the vector $A\mathbf{v}.$
examples.worked_solution:
The eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14056271/assets/bf65510b8cef0e0162e3054bcf31405ac4e4268a759f6493a06c9f0314c1d482.png) corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda=2.$ So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}Av=2v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following picture:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14056271/assets/78e1e3c015adad2c826a64e255bd982941dc9fe50679acc2bae3f00b31bd9f39.png)

feedback.problem:
Determine if $v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -6 \\ 3 & 10\end{aligned}].$
If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?
feedback.worked_solution:
The eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -6 \\ 3 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =4\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =4v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=4v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =4.$
